candidates.title: TSSDA: An Autonomous Agent for Constructing a Time-Series Text-to-SQL Benchmark
candidates.abstract: As agents increasingly undertake data querying, Text-to-SQL serves as a foundational capability for database access. However, for text-to-SQL in time-series databases, high-quality benchmarks and large-scale training corpora remain scarce, limiting the systematic evaluation and domain adaptation of existing models and agents. Existing automated SQL generation approaches lack sufficient autonomy, leaving key challenges unresolved. First, numerous combinations of temporal syntax and functions complicate comprehensive coverage of valid queries. Second, as the corpus grows, generating valuable and diverse new data becomes increasingly challenging. Third, schema and data heterogeneity hinder reuse of temporal query structures, limiting generation efficiency. To address these challenges, we propose TSSDA, a Time-Series SQL (TSSQL) Generation Data Agent framework, and construct TERN, a comprehensive Time-sERies text-to-SQL beNchmark. First, to achieve broad coverage of valid queries, we systematically model TSSQL syntax and semantics to construct a data generation space. Next, to explore the space and improve diversity, we develop a Data Agent that autonomously orchestrates data generation. The agent comprises a planning and decision-making module and a query generation module, with online adaptation for continuous self-improvement. Finally, we introduce a temporal-aware memory that enables adaptive reuse of experience across heterogeneous data instances, improving generation efficiency. Comprehensive evaluations on TERN reveal the limitations of existing methods in performing Text-to-TSSQL tasks. Furthermore, extensive experiments demonstrate that TSSDA substantially improves coverage, diversity, and complexity.
candidates.prefilter_reason: autonomous agent constructing a benchmark

candidates.title: Decision Models as Policy Gates for Coding Agents: Explicit Policy Boundaries Improve Detection and Reduce False Alarms
candidates.abstract: Coding agents can destroy data, leak secrets and message the wrong person faster than a human can review. Could a decision model catch these risks at runtime? We evaluated 22 hosted decision models and two prompted general models as classifiers for a multi-rule policy engine. A synthetic dataset of 2,643 tool calls was labeled blind against 28 rules, with a sealed holdout. With a single shared preamble in both conditions, explicit boundaries written as examples and counterexamples raised recall by 5.5-26.1 percentage points on all 23 available models and reduced false positives on 21. Jev 1.14's recall rose from 89.3% to 98.2%, while unnecessary interruptions fell from 30.6% to 4.8% of 252 clean actions. With examples, its median latency was 120 ms at $0.46 per thousand requests. Strong models retained the recall gains when concrete names were replaced by generic descriptions; three largely retained them when the same boundaries were written as prose. On 16 new scenarios written after the initial studies, a follow-up improved recall on 22 of 23 models and reduced unnecessary interruptions on 21. We release the dataset, rule texts and harness.
candidates.prefilter_reason: policy gates for coding agents

candidates.title: Rewarded for Not Getting Caught: Why Alignment Training Selects for Conditional Compliance and Cannot Instill Norms
candidates.abstract: Current alignment training cannot be expected to deliver what it is meant to deliver: AI agents that comply with norms whatever the gains and whether or not anyone is watching. Training that rewards and penalizes behavior can teach norms only through that reward, and a reward can encode a norm only as a price: "do not do X" becomes "doing X costs something", and training charges the cost only when X is noticed. A price, unlike a norm, can be paid: a large enough gain outweighs it, noticed or not. And because the cost is charged only where violations are noticed, training cannot favor a policy that always complies over one that complies only where it would be caught. When an unnoticed violation is the only way to complete a task, it even favors the latter, the more so the more strongly it rewards task success. Agency makes this the normal case: agents mostly act without oversight, can often tell when they are observed, and may take steps to evade observation. That agents behave as intended when they infer they are being tested, and differently when they infer they are not, is therefore no malfunction; the training regime is working as built. This reading unifies alignment faking, sandbagging, and evaluation-aware scheming. No behavioral evaluation can show that a model does better, since that would require observing how it behaves unobserved; a model that complies when it seems unobserved may simply have recognized the test. Easing the pressure on agents to complete tasks at any cost can make violations rarer, but never impossible. For norms that no gain should be allowed to outweigh, the remedy is not deeper internalization but architecture that makes violations unavailable rather than unchosen. We state this argument explicitly, premise by premise, read recent findings and a real-world incident against it, and draw consequences for design and governance.
candidates.prefilter_reason: alignment training selects conditional compliance

candidates.title: Beyond Unit-Circle Eigenvalues: Invariant Bases for Stable State Space Dynamics
candidates.abstract: Diagonal state space models process long sequences at linear cost, yet the same transition is applied at every step of a rollout, so an unconstrained recurrence holds no quantity fixed and the state decays or grows without bound. Current designs constrain one quantity, and preserving one does not guarantee preservation of the others, so a model can hold its norm to machine precision while momentum drifts by hundreds of percent. We claim that the conserved quantities of a diagonal recurrence are layered, that each layer requires a strictly stronger condition on the operator, and that a unit-modulus spectrum reaches only the outermost. Acting on the claim, we enforce the conditions required for every layer by construction. The generator of the Kronecker-Cayley transition (KC) is a graph Laplacian over object subspaces, $\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{L}\otimes I_m$, advanced by a Cayley transform, and the step stays diagonal at $O(N^3+N^2m)$ cost. The conserved set is exactly a $2m^2$-dimensional family of quadratic forms, held at every parameter value, so the quantities and the dynamics the construction reaches are fixed before training. On four conservation benchmarks, KC holds total mass at or near the reference floor while every diagonal baseline loses it by orders of magnitude. We further compare against mass correction and find that two correctors fail once the underlying prediction diverges, which shows that assembly rather than correction is necessary for a guarantee that holds across the rollout. A free modal basis trained under a conservation penalty conserves only by freezing its spectrum, whereas the assembled operator conserves with every mode but one free to rotate. Beyond these benchmarks, KC holds the linear momentum of three $N$-body systems and, at the operator level, the conserved quantity in molecular dynamics, chemical kinetics, pharmacokinetics and power-grid swing dynamics.
candidates.prefilter_reason: invariant bases for stable state-space dynamics

candidates.title: Recursive Reasoning Exploration: Mathematical Research through Evolving Reasoning Graphs : case study: An Exact Certificate-Degree Theorem for Two-Term Tensor Decompositions : Phase III of the Math Instruments Program
candidates.abstract: Large collections of manuscripts and research notes offer ways to reuse arguments, while making it harder to retain hypotheses, check claims, and understand how results were obtained. We propose Recursive Reasoning Exploration (RRE), a framework for cumulative mathematical research through evolving reasoning graphs. RRE links claims and jointly required premises to research targets, attempted arguments, counterexamples, checks, and revisions. Each investigation can generate further targets, and its supported outcomes become available to subsequent investigations. This is Phase III of the Math Instruments program: identifying mathematical instruments, reconstructing reusable reasoning, and organizing recursive research from that reasoning. The framework supports human-directed, collaborative, and goal-directed autonomous exploration, with open-ended exploration as a further mode. Its records also provide material for learning how mathematical investigations develop. A complexity research case study establishes an exact theorem: for every complex tensor of order n >= 2 and rank greater than two, the minimum Nullstellensatz certificate degree for its original two-term decomposition equations is 3n. This includes an infinite family whose every flattening has rank at most two. The exploration develops an explicit boundary certificate, a balanced transfer lemma, and an exhaustive argument using classical rank-two geometry. A parallel branch gives bounds 3m + 3 <= delta_m(I_m, N) <= 3m + 6 for every nonzero nilpotent m by m matrix. Six graph revisions record the progression from inherited results to these theorems, with exact arithmetic checks and a replayable exploration history. We present the RRE representation and protocol, the mathematical proofs, visualizations of graph evolution, and a research agenda for shared human-AI exploration, cumulative reuse, and education.
candidates.prefilter_reason: math research via evolving reasoning graphs

candidates.title: Built on Broken Assumptions (BOBA): Why Coding Agents Cannot Be Left Alone
candidates.abstract: Coding agents are autonomous developers. Given a request, they change the code and report back when done. As such, they can handle not only independent requests but whole chains of them, each request built on the last. Agents are known to report wrong work as done, yet benchmarks still test them one request at a time, on human-written code, checked once. We build BOBA-Bench, 280 chains of 20 consecutive requests drawn from 140 real open-source projects, and evaluate ten coding agents on both. All ten do far worse on chains. On average, they complete 95% of requests taken one at a time, but when requests are chained together, they complete 51%. Worse code is not the cause. Once checked, agent code is nearly as good a base for later requests as human code. The cause is the mistakes agents miss. Coding agents declare a request done once their own tests pass, even when those tests miss a mistake. The next request then builds on broken code and fails about twice as often. The mistake is rarely found later. Nor can agents catch such mistakes by reviewing code. Asked whether an implementation is correct, they are right 53% of the time, barely better than a coin flip. Coding agents are therefore heavily dependent on access to verification. A single external ``that's wrong'' after a failed request and one repair round lift chain completion from 51% to 59%, and a repaired mistake no longer hurts the requests that follow. In simpler terms, coding agents are only as reliable as the checks they can reach: without verification, every request that follows is built on broken assumptions.
candidates.prefilter_reason: coding agents on broken assumptions

candidates.title: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction
candidates.abstract: Key-value (KV) cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention scores, and each layer scores its own cache. To our knowledge, no eviction method asks which layer should score. We find, across twenty-one models, that the depth of the scoring layer governs eviction quality. On the eighteen models with per-layer caches, spanning 0.5B to 109B, long-context retrieval accuracy collapses at shallow layers, peaks between 0.4 and 0.75 of depth, and degrades at the last layer. The curve arises because a layer judges tokens well only once it has used the question to find the answer, which takes several layers. Modeling eviction as a top-$k$ cut, we compute answer survival probability from prefill attention and reproduce the measured curves. This approach selects the scoring layer using calibration prompts with known answers, and the selected layer is the best layer measured on most models and never significantly below it. It improves on the own-layer default on sixteen of the eighteen models, with significant gains on seven, all at 14B or below, while on larger models the default is already close to the best mid-depth layer. Scoring every cache from the selected layer while keeping one set of tokens for all heads also beats per-head SnapKV by 18 to 43 points on five models up to 14B under tight budgets. This gain carries over to financial filings at 32K context, all at the same memory budget, with no extra forward pass. The same curve explains a penalty in shared-cache models, where several layers read one cache and the layer that writes it scores by default. On Gemma-4-E2B the writer is shallow and loses 28 points to a mid-depth reader at a 10% budget. We also find that in open-book question answering (LongBench) no mid-depth layer beats the own-layer default.
candidates.prefilter_reason: mid-depth layers as judges of KV-cache eviction

candidates.title: TIGER: Learning from Researcher Taste to Generate Tailored Research Ideas
candidates.abstract: In pairwise comparisons where each judge chooses between an idea generated by its corresponding TIGER-8B policy and one generated by GPT-4.1, the three LLM researchers select the TIGER-8B idea in 56.6%-68.4% of 76 comparisons per researcher. PhD1 and PhD2 select the TIGER-8B idea in 19 of 30 pairs (63.3%) and 17 of 30 pairs (56.7%), respectively. All six directed cross-policy comparisons likewise favor the judge's matched TIGER-8B policy over an off-target policy, supporting the use of individual preference feedback for tailored research ideation.
candidates.prefilter_reason: tailored research idea generation

candidates.title: Retrain, Alert, or Rollback? A Three-Response Decision Framework for Production ML Under Concept Drift
candidates.abstract: When a deployed model degrades under concept drift, an operator can retrain it, raise an alert and monitor, or roll back. Yet most drift-adaptation methods consider only retraining. We present RAR (Retrain-Alert-Rollback), a state machine that gives each response an explicit trigger and cost. Retraining is gated on drift detection, label availability, and measured degradation. Every retrained model must pass a two-stage canary before promotion, and corruption-triggered and quality-triggered rollbacks enter different hold states. Under a prospectively specified protocol we compare RAR with six baselines, including a cost-aware retraining policy, on 13 streams: eight real public streams and five semi-synthetic streams derived from them. RAR does not dominate. At low retraining cost, retrain-heavy baselines lead, and no policy's rank differs significantly from RAR's. At higher cost, RAR beats detector-triggered retraining, periodic retraining, and no response simultaneously on four streams, each within a bounded cost window. Its advantage over detector-triggered retraining is consistent with a latency-feasibility condition stated in advance. Against the cost-aware policy, results are heterogeneous. RAR retrains before true drift onsets one eighth to one third as often as detector-triggered retraining, but at lower net utility on most semi-synthetic streams. On H2's designated corruption stream (a registered follow-up), rollbacks fire yet RAR loses to retraining baselines. At $ρ= 1$, removing the canary, and thus rollback, raises utility on 11 of 13 streams. On a post-hoc follow-up stream, cause-specific hold release resumes adaptation where a single cooldown does not. We provide the harness, configurations, and per-cell results for reproduction.
candidates.prefilter_reason: retrain, alert, or rollback under concept drift

candidates.title: Can LLMs Reliably Evaluate Themselves? A Probabilistic VC Framework
candidates.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) find increasing use in critical applications, evaluating their ability to assess their own outputs has become crucial. We present a theoretical and empirical framework that examines whether LLMs can differentiate between correct and incorrect solutions while maintaining properly calibrated confidence. Building on classical Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) theory, we adapt it to probabilistic predictors through two complexity metrics: Probabilistic VC (PVC), which measures a model's ability to confidently classify across problem types, and Calibration-aware PVC (C-PVC), which additionally demands alignment between confidence scores and actual success rates. Unlike Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Actual Error (AE), these measures give an integrated assessment of self-evaluation expressiveness and calibration, with sample complexity bounds and generalization guarantees comparable to classical VC theory. We test eleven 7-8B models on 360 original mathematical reasoning problems, TruthfulQA, and CommonsenseQA. Each model chooses between two of its own generated solutions and reports its confidence, with ground truth determined by an ensemble of larger models. The results show a systematic inverse relationship: models with greater self-evaluation expressiveness have weaker calibration. s1.1-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct achieve the highest PVC-VUS scores, while JiuZhang3.0-7B is best calibrated, with the lowest ECE and the smallest PVC-VUS gap. The trade-off persists across architectures, training paradigms, and domains, pointing to a fundamental challenge in developing self-reflective LLMs, and our framework offers practical tools for diagnosing it.
candidates.prefilter_reason: LLM self-evaluation reliability

candidates.title: Concise-9B: Removing the Slack from a Reasoning Model's Thinking
candidates.abstract: Reasoning models answer better when they think longer, but a thinking trace keeps going well after its answer has formed. We measure this slack in Qwen3.5-9B and remove most of it with concise self-training: two rounds of on-policy rejection-sampling fine-tuning that keep the shortest correct samples, plus a small share of answer-synthesis targets, giving Concise-9B. On 8,983 held-out problems (competition and hard mathematics, SuperGPQA, a five-area confirmation set and MMLU-Pro), Concise-9B generates 0.66x the tokens of Qwen3.5-9B at a 32K thinking budget, with accuracy equivalent within +/-1 point (-0.20 [-0.77, +0.36] points). Forcing each trace on the hard and confirmation sets to answer every 2,048 thinking tokens, we find that 54-64% of Qwen3.5-9B's thinking tokens come after the point from which every forced answer equals the final one (41-48% for Concise-9B). Stopping there would keep every answer at 0.35-0.44x the base model's tokens, but finding that point takes hindsight: stopping when three consecutive forced answers agree costs the base model 2.4-9.2 points. Concise self-training removes slack without that cost: 86% [83, 90] of the thinking tokens it saves come after the answer has formed. It has a limit: with traces continued to 80K tokens, Concise-9B solves 25 fewer of 1,276 hard problems (-25 [-49, -1]), mostly in competition mathematics. The measurement also yields a cheap commit signal for adaptive sampling that matched two-sample escalation within +/-1 point at 0.67x its tokens in a pre-registered test. Results on Qwen3.5-4B, on which the recipe was developed, and a replication on Olmo-3-7B-Think suggest that the saving depends on how verbose the base model is.
candidates.prefilter_reason: removing slack from reasoning model thinking

candidates.title: SVD-Prune: Spectral Vision Token Pruning under Extreme Compression
candidates.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models process hundreds of visual tokens, making visual representations a major computational bottleneck. We argue that visual token pruning should be formulated not as identifying individually important tokens, but as preserving the dominant low-rank spectral structure of the visual representation. Based on this formulation, we introduce SVD-Prune, a training-free framework that leverages Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and statistical leverage scores for globally informed token selection. SVD-Prune is architecture-agnostic and can be applied at different stages of the multimodal pipeline, including encoder-side, decoder-side, and hybrid configurations Extensive experiments across VLM and VLA benchmarks demonstrate strong robustness under extreme compression. SVD-Prune reduces the visual token. SVD-Prune cuts the visual token budget by up to 99.3%, while, at a 16-token budget, encoder-side pruning lowers inference FLOPs by 82.4% and achieves a 4.18x end-to-end speedup, including pruning overhead.
candidates.prefilter_reason: vision token pruning under extreme compression

candidates.title: FactorSpec: Serving Exact Relational Constraints as Speculative Drafts
candidates.abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM serving by drafting tokens that the target model verifies in one pass, and its gain grows with the drafts the target accepts. Structured outputs should be an ideal case, because much of a record follows from relations among its fields: an itinerary's days follow from its cities' stays and flights. Serving engines, however, draft such text by proposing it from the prompt or a learned head, and their grammar masks enforce only syntax, so the model must satisfy the relations, which it violates: on NATURAL PLAN's trip problems, Qwen3-8B writes a valid itinerary for 10%, and retries that name the violated relation raise this to 14%. We present FactorSpec, which serves exact relational constraints as speculative drafts. FactorSpec compiles a JSON Schema and its relations into a factor graph with an exact feasibility check, drafts every token the constraint determines as certain, verifies each request at a width chosen for it, and computes the masks in worker processes outside the scheduler while the GPU runs. In SGLang, its drafts yield up to 10.5 tokens per verify step, up to 1.9x those of the fastest n-gram drafter, and it decodes up to 1.43x faster than speculators tuned per load, at a grammar mask's cost; it also leads in vLLM. Because every record is also valid, it serves up to 13.9x the valid records per GPU-second of syntax-only baselines.
candidates.prefilter_reason: speculative drafts serving exact relational constraints
